The Qing Dynasty. From 1644 to 1912 CE, the Qing was the final imperial dynasty of China, established by the Manchus, a Jurchen people from Manchuria, after they conquered the collapsing Ming Dynasty. Despite being foreign conquerors, the Manchus adopted Han Chinese governance, language, and ideology so thoroughly that they appeared to be the restorers of Chinese civilization itself, a triumph of cultural absorption over military victory. The dynasty reached its greatest territorial extent under Emperor Kangxi, who reigned from 1661 to 1722 CE, and his successor Yongzheng, establishing Qing dominance over Tibet, Mongolia, Xinjiang, and Taiwan. However, the nineteenth century brought catastrophe: European imperial powers, armed with superior military technology, forcibly opened China through the Opium Wars, unequal treaties, and spheres of influence. The Qing's inability to modernize or resist Western aggression led to its collapse in 1912 CE, ending nearly two thousand years of imperial rule.

The Manchus invaded from Manchuria under the Dorgon regency, acting for the child emperor Shunzhi, and conquered China by 1683 CE. Emperor Kangxi, one of China's greatest rulers, consolidated Qing power and expanded the empire to its greatest territorial extent. The Manchus adopted Han governance structures, Confucian ideology, and the civil-service examination system; they portrayed themselves as custodians of Chinese civilization.

The Qing annexed Mongolia and established hegemony over the Khalkha Mongols in 1691 CE. They brought Tibet under Qing protection through military campaigns and the elevation of the Dalai Lama as a spiritual, not political, authority. They conquered Xinjiang and Taiwan, extending the empire to its greatest territorial scope, nearly the entire territory of modern China. The Qing established tributary relationships with neighboring states including Korea, Vietnam, Siam, and Burma, demanding recognition of Qing supremacy.

The Manchus adopted Han dress, language, and Confucian philosophy; intermarriage between Manchus and Han was initially forbidden, then gradually permitted. They imposed the Manchu queue, braided hair, as a symbol of Manchu dominance. Han Chinese, forced to wear it, resented this mark of subjugation. Despite deep cultural integration, the Han scholar class remained ambivalent about Manchu rule; resistance movements periodically erupted.

Kangxi's long reign of sixty-one years saw stability, economic growth, and cultural flourishing. Emperor Yongzheng, who reigned from 1722 to 1735 CE, and Emperor Qianlong, who reigned from 1735 to 1796 CE, continued expansion and refined the bureaucracy. Population grew from approximately one hundred million to approximately three hundred million; agriculture and trade flourished. Qing ceramics, painting, and literature reached refinement; the Kangxi dictionary was a monumental scholarly achievement.

The Qing sponsored the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, an encyclopedic collection of classical Chinese texts, a monument to Confucian learning. Qing landscape painting carried forward Ming traditions while developing new styles emphasizing personal expression. Qing porcelain maintained high standards set by Ming; intricate famille-rose enamels and underglaze blue designs were globally prized.

For most of the Qing era, China viewed Western barbarians with indifference or disdain and maintained strict control of trade through the Canton System. The Macartney Embassy in 1793 CE saw British envoy Lord Macartney travel to Qianlong's court seeking to expand trade. Qianlong refused, believing China needed nothing from the West.

Britain forcibly opened China to the opium trade in the First Opium War from 1840 to 1842 CE. China's defeat exposed military and technological inferiority. The Treaty of Nanking in 1842 CE forced China to cede Hong Kong, open five ports, and pay reparations. Britain and France defeated China again in the Second Opium War from 1856 to 1860 CE, forcing even greater concessions. Unequal treaties stripped China of sovereignty: foreign powers gained extraterritorial rights, most-favored-nation status, and control of tariffs.

The Taiping Rebellion from 1850 to 1864 CE killed millions and devastated the south; Qing recovery was slow. Reformers attempted to modernize the military and economy through the Self-Strengthening Movement, but Qing conservatism and elite resistance stifled efforts. China was defeated by Japan in the First Sino-Japanese War from 1894 to 1895 CE, shocking China and accelerating reform movements. The Boxer Rebellion from 1899 to 1901 CE was an anti-Western peasant uprising crushed by an international coalition; Qing weakness to the world became undeniable. The Chinese Revolution from 1911 to 1912 CE, a republican revolution under Sun Yat-sen, overthrew the Qing; the dynasty formally abdicated in 1912 CE.

The Qing Dynasty embodied a fundamental paradox: successful cultural conquest coupled with military and technological obsolescence in the face of Western power. For much of the Qing era, China remained the world's wealthiest and most populous civilization; Kangxi and Qianlong ruled vast, stable, prosperous empires. Yet this success bred complacency. While Europeans developed steam power, industrialization, and modern military technology, Qing elites, confident in their cultural superiority, stagnated. The Opium Wars shattered China's illusion of superiority and initiated a century of national humiliation, foreign domination, and internal strife. The Qing's inability to modernize while preserving its cosmological worldview doomed it. The dynasty's fall ended not just a political regime but an entire worldview: the belief that China was the center of civilization and that Western barbarians were inherently inferior.
